commands.name: kntnt
commands.description: Manage this collection — which skills are Enabled, in Global and in each Project. (user)

commands.name: proofread
commands.description: Correct only mechanical language errors — spelling, grammar, punctuation, agreement, inflection, duplicated or missing words, and locale mechanics — in one supplied text, preserving its wording, meaning, tone, structure, formatting, and metadata. Start it on your own only when a specific text is at hand and the request either uses a proofreading term (proofread, spell-check, copyedit, fix the typos, korrekturläs, rätta stavfelen) or is unambiguously limited to mechanical language errors. Not for a request to edit, rewrite, polish, improve, tighten, or review a text — each of those asks for changes this Skill refuses to make. A user may also invoke it by name at any time. (user)

commands.name: redline
commands.description: Review one supplied text against this collection's editorial contract — its genre, its optional technique, its language, and the shared anti-slop catalogue — and, when selected, a Writing Brief; repair what the review found through a bounded budget of fresh correction subagents, report whatever is left unresolved, and finish with exactly one mechanical pass. (user)

commands.name: unslop
commands.description: Apply this collection's anti-slop pass to one supplied text and nothing else — false contrasts, empty openings, importance inflation, vague attribution, synonym cycling, robotic rhythm, and generic conclusions — repairing what it finds through a bounded budget of fresh correction subagents and reporting whatever is left. It selects no genre, no technique, and no editorial contract, and it runs no mechanical pass. (user)

commands.name: write
commands.description: Turn a brief and its source material into one truthful first draft in the target language, and stop there. Start it on your own only when the literal token `/write` appears in the request or in an instruction the request points at — inside a longer message, a document, or a checklist that says to run it. Not for a bare request to write, draft, compose, summarise, rewrite, edit, or review something — without `/write` in it, such a request is answered as it otherwise would be. A user may also invoke it by name at any time. (user)

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: no-ai-slop
commands.description: Edit drafts into sharper, more human writing while preserving the writer's personal voice, or detect AI-slop patterns without rewriting. Use when the user wants a draft clearer, more direct, more opinionated, or less AI-sounding, or asks whether writing reads as AI. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: teach
commands.description: Teach the user a new skill or concept, within this workspace. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: schedule
commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

commands.name: workflow-authoring
commands.description: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.

commands.name: run
commands.description: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

commands.name: run-skill-generator
commands.description: Author or improve the run-<unit> skill - a per-project skill that tells agents how to build, launch, and drive this project's app. Use when the user asks to set up the project, get it running, write run instructions, or verify build/run steps work from a clean environment.

     1	# Ten minutes on a Friday
     2	
     3	For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.
     4	
     5	The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.
     6	
     7	In March she tried something else: a session every Friday. "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea."
     8	
     9	It works like this. She photographs each receipt when she gets it, while it is still new and readable. On Friday she sits down with the week's photographs, matches each one to a line in her bank account and makes a note of anything odd, such as a payment she does not recognise or a receipt with no bank line at all. The app reads the date, the supplier and the total from each photograph and suggests the bank line it matches.
    10	
    11	Our users see the same pattern. In a survey this summer, 412 of them told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts at least once a week reported a median of 6 hours. Those who left receipts until January reported 19. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show that the habit caused the difference. But they point the same way as Priya's January.
    12	
    13	"January this year was an evening," she says.
    14	
    15	The tin is still on the shelf. These days it holds tea bags, and the receipts in her phone are all readable.

     9	
    10	Invented evaluation material. Larkspur Ledger and every person named are fictional and describe no real company or client.
    11	
    12	## 1. What is the assignment?
    13	
    14	- Working title: Ten minutes on a Friday
    15	- Topic: keeping receipts in order through the tax year.
    16	- Genre: general, a letter-length piece for the newsletter.
    17	- Channel: Larkspur Ledger's monthly newsletter to sole traders.
    18	- Language: en_GB, one version only.
    19	- Length: roughly 300 to 450 words.
    20	- Search phrase: none, deliberately; the newsletter is not found through search.
    21	
    22	## 2. Which brand is the sender?
    23	
    24	Larkspur Ledger, a bookkeeping app for sole traders in the UK. Promise: bookkeeping that takes minutes, not weekends. Image: known to its users as practical; most newsletter readers are on the free plan and have not tried the receipt scanner. Mandate: bookkeeping habits and its own app; it gives no tax advice. Tone of voice: plain, friendly, a little dry. Tone in this text: the same; a newsletter piece has room for the dry humour, so the brand and the genre pull the same way.
    25	
    26	## 3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?
    27	
    28	Larkspur Ledger's receipt scanner turns a weekly receipt session into a ten-minute job. The message need not appear in the text: the piece leads the reader to the weekly habit, and the reader, who already has the app, sees where the scanner fits.
    29	
    30	## 4. Who is the reader?
    31	
    32	Sole traders such as tutors, plumbers and designers who use the app's free plan and file their own Self Assessment return. They know the return is due on 31 January and that receipts matter, but most keep them in a drawer or an inbox until January. They care about their time and about not losing expenses they could have claimed. Why now: the newsletter goes out in early October, with the second half of the tax year starting and time left to change the habit before January.
    33	
    34	## 5. What is the text's angle?
    35	
    36	The weekly habit as what makes January short: what a sole trader gains by spending ten minutes on receipts every Friday instead of a weekend in January.
    37	
    38	## 6. What is the hook?
    39	
    40	The last weekend of January spent with a tin of faded receipts, and the expenses that go unclaimed because a receipt has faded to blank.
    41	
    42	## 7. How should the text be structured?
    43	
    44	ABT.
    45	
    46	The whole text in one sentence: a sole trader keeps receipts through the year and files the return in January, and if the receipts are in order the return is a short job, but most leave them in a drawer because sorting feels like a job for later, and faded receipts and a lost weekend are the price, therefore the text shows that ten minutes every Friday makes the return short, by walking through one Friday session.
    47	
    48	Sketch:
    49	
    50	1. And: the return is due on 31 January, and receipts pile up in a drawer or an inbox until then.
    51	2. But: till receipts fade within months, and expenses without a readable receipt go unclaimed. The survey: those who match receipts weekly report a median of 6 hours on the return, against 19 hours for those who wait until January (source 1).
    52	3. Therefore, part 1: what a Friday session looks like: photograph the week's receipts, match each to a bank line, note anything odd.
    53	4. Therefore, part 2: Priya Nand, a tutor, who moved to a Friday session in March (source 2).
    54	5. The ending: back to the tin of receipts, which this January is empty.
    55	
    56	## 8. What should be left out?
    57	
    58	No tax advice, and no claims about which expenses are allowable. No comparison with other apps. No prices and no mention of the paid plan.
    59	
    60	## 9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?
    61	
    62	Ten minutes on receipts every Friday turns the January return from a lost weekend into a short job.
    63	
    64	## 10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?
    65	
    66	- Main effect: the reader starts a weekly receipt habit.
    67	- The way there: the reader first needs to believe that a weekly session is short.
    68	- Call to action and measure: indirect. The text does not ask; the reader is left wanting to start this Friday and knowing the steps. Measure: the share of newsletter readers who scan a receipt in the week after it goes out.
    69	
    70	## 11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?
    71	
    72	- Relevant: the October send-out with January ahead, in step 1 and the ending.
    73	- Interesting: the hook, the January weekend and the faded receipts, in steps 1 and 2.
    74	- Valuable: the steps of a Friday session in step 3, and Priya's example in step 4.
    75	
    76	Chain check:
    77	
    78	- Does the reader follow from the sender and the channel? Yes, the newsletter goes to the app's sole traders.
    79	- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle? Yes, every reader knows the January weekend.
    80	- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length? Yes, five steps fit the length.
    81	- Is the conclusion what the structure actually lands in, does it carry the message, and does it lie within the brand's mandate? Yes; the weekly habit is where the scanner fits, and a habit is within the mandate.
    82	- Does what the reader understands lead to the effect you have described, and does that effect serve the brand's goals? Yes.
    83	- Does anything in the structure conflict with what should be left out? No.
    84	
    85	## 12. What sources do you know of, and what do you need to find out?
    86	
    87	1. Larkspur Ledger's user survey, summer 2026, in `material.md`.
    88	2. The interview with Priya Nand, in `material.md`.
    89	3. The support team's note on till receipts and the scanner, in `material.md`.
    90	
    91	Nothing is left to find out.

Installed 1 package in 1ms
{
  "selector": "en_GB",
  "code": "en_GB",
  "language": "English",
  "territory": "GB",
  "territory_name": "United Kingdom",
  "inherits": null,
  "scopes": {
    "composition": {
      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "British general-interest prose is understated. It states a strong claim plainly and lets the claim carry the emphasis, where American register would reach for an intensifier. Irony and litotes are available and are not read as evasion.

Collective nouns take plural agreement when the members are acting and singular when the body is acting as one: *the team are arguing about it*, *the committee has published its report*. Both are correct; what matters is that the choice is consistent within a passage.

The present perfect covers a recent past that still bears on now: *I've just seen the figures*, *have you eaten?* The simple past in those positions reads as American.

*Have got* is ordinary British usage for possession and obligation — *I've got the file*, *you've got to see this* — and is not an informality to be edited out of general prose.

Prepositions differ in a small, fixed set of places: *at the weekend*, *in hospital*, *different from* or *different to*, *write to somebody*, *meet somebody* rather than *meet with*. None of these is a preference; each is the British form.

Spelling is *-ise* or *-ize* by house style — both are correct British English, *-ise* being the majority convention and *-ize* the Oxford one — but a document uses one throughout. The *-yse* group is invariant: *analyse*, *paralyse*, *catalyse*, in Oxford spelling as in any other.

Quotation marks are single as the outer mark in most British house styles, with double inside; some publications invert this. Follow the document's own choice and make it consistent."
    },
    "review": {
      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "Read for American vocabulary that has drifted in: *gotten*, *math*, *fall* for autumn, *elevator*, *sidewalk*, *movie theater*, *diaper*, *vacation*, *check* for a restaurant bill. A single one is a slip; a scatter of them means the text was drafted in another variety.

Read for mixed formats in one document — dates written both *24 August 2026* and *August 24, 2026*, currency in both *£* and *$*, times in both *2.30pm* and *2:30 p.m.* Format drift is the clearest evidence of assembly from several sources.

Check *-ise* and *-ize* consistency across the whole document, not paragraph by paragraph. Generated British English is frequently American English with some suffixes changed, and the ones that were missed are where it shows.

British institutional and business prose slides into passive nominal style: *It is anticipated that a review will be undertaken*. Give it back its subject and its verb: *We expect to review it*.

Watch for hedges in chains — *somewhat rather more likely*, *it may perhaps be the case that* — where British understatement has stopped being restraint and become evasion. One hedge does work; three cancel each other.

Check that punctuation inside and outside quotation marks follows one convention. British practice places a mark inside the quotation only when it belongs to the quoted matter.

Check title capitalisation is one system throughout. British house styles differ over whether headings take sentence case or title case, and a document that alternates has chosen neither."
    },
    "anti-slop": {
      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "The reskinning tell. Generated British English is very often American English with a spelling pass over it, so the vocabulary and the format are what give it away rather than the spelling: *colour* and *organisation* in a text that still writes *gotten*, *2:30 p.m.*, and *$*.

*Whilst*, *amongst*, *utilise*, *endeavour*, and *commence* sprinkled through ordinary prose. Each exists; none is the neutral British choice, and their density is a model reaching for something that sounds British rather than something a British writer would write. *While*, *among*, *use*, *try*, and *start* are the words.

Suffix inconsistency inside one text — *organise* in one paragraph and *recognize* in the next — is a generation artefact rather than a style, and it is worth naming as such rather than silently normalising, because it usually means the passage came from somewhere else.

A concentration of punctuation forms that conflict with the document's convention is a generation tell. Refer to Mechanics for the conventions; this scope does not restate them.

The apologetic opening: *It is perhaps worth noting that*, *One might argue that*, *It would be fair to say that*. British hedging turned into an opening formula that says nothing before the sentence starts."
    }
  }
}

# Delivery

Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, how a response carries the text, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in and whether what those words say is true of the text they name, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.

## The response is the default

The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.

A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.

An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.

## How a response carries the text

A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.

The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.

The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.

Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.

The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. A response-targeted run that changed nothing and has findings left fences the artifact like any other; a run that stopped before it could deliver and carries its preserved prose in the reply fences that prose, and says in its own words outside the fence what the prose has not been through. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.

## An explicit destination

An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.

**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.

**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.

**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.

## Deriving a filename for a directory

A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.

That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.

A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.

## What the response carries when a destination was named

A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.

That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.

## In-place Editing

In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.

A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. The brief, the interview, the notes, and the article it draws on are where the text came from and not where it goes; a Skill that could overwrite them would make supplying a file a risk rather than a convenience, and would lose the material the result is answerable to.

In-place Editing requires exactly one writable local source file, and it is mutually exclusive with a separate output option. A run replaces its source or delivers elsewhere, never both, and an invocation asking for both has named two destinations for one text.

It is refused wherever there is no such file to replace. Text supplied inline in the invocation or taken from the conversation is not a file. A URL is not a local file, and fetching one grants no right to write anything back. An uploaded source and a read-only file cannot be replaced. More than one Text Artifact leaves the single file the contract is written around undefined.

An explicit output path equal to the input path is refused in favour of In-place Editing, and the refusal says which gesture to use. Replacing a source then has one recognizable authorization: a reader of an invocation sees that a source is about to be replaced from the request itself, without comparing two paths to discover it.

## When nothing changed

A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.

A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.

An in-place run that changed nothing leaves the source file untouched and returns the short status with any unresolved findings. Rewriting a file with its own contents would make its timestamp claim that something happened.

That status is written in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, so a Swedish text that needed no work is reported on in Swedish.

An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. Creating that artifact is what was asked for, and a destination left empty because the text needed no work is a request refused without saying so. A directory destination derives its filename and resolves collisions exactly as it would for a changed text, and the response reports the destination without repeating the artifact beside it, exactly as for a run that changed something.

## The language of a report about the text

A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. So a Swedish artifact reviewed from an English-language invocation comes back with Swedish findings, whether the run corrected anything or was asked to correct nothing at all, and one text never produces a status in its own language beside a finding list in another.

Who reads it is what decides this. A report about a text is read by the reader of that text, who has to finish whatever the run left undone, and a report in whichever language the invocation happened to be written in reaches that reader in a language nothing about the text promised. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.

## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.

## Refusals

Every contradictory, meaningless, or unusable output request is refused before the first side effect. The cases this contract names are more than one Text Artifact where the Skill processes one, an output option together with In-place Editing, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing for inline text or a URL or an uploaded or read-only source, and a destination the run cannot write — a path whose parent directory does not exist among them.

Every such check that can be made by reading is made before anything is written, so a refusal leaves no partial effect behind: no file created, none truncated, none renamed, and no directory made. Where a conflict can only be discovered after a legitimate effect, the run stops there and reports the exact partial outcome rather than continuing.

A refusal follows the Collection's ordinary diagnostic and help conventions. It names what was wrong, prints the synopsis of the most specific recognized command page verbatim, and points at that command's own help form. An output option is refused rather than ignored where it has no work to do, a flag accepted and ignored teaching that flags sometimes do nothing.

# Questions to answer before you write

The Writing Brief template: each numbered question carries the guidance for answering it. This English reference is authoritative; render its questions and guidance in the user's working language while retaining every question, its number and its order. Its genre and technique examples explain the form, not what is installed: the Library directories supply those choices, and where a genre and this guidance differ, the genre governs.

How to use the template: answer the questions in full sentences and as concretely as you can. The details under the assignment may be short. You may fill in the questions in whatever order suits you, but the order below is the one the brief is read in. It runs from what the assignment gives you, through the context and the shape of the text, to a check that everything holds together. When every answer is there, you have a brief. If you cannot answer a question, you need to find out more before you start writing. Sources and evidence, on the other hand, can be added during the work. Refer to other answers by name, for example "the message" or "the hook", not by the question's number.

## 1. What is the assignment?

Here you gather what the assignment gives you. Most of it needs no thinking up, but it governs everything that follows.

- **Working title:** a name for the text, so that everyone immediately remembers what it is about. It need not be punchy, effective or even accurate. It only needs to be short and clear.
- **Topic:** what the text is about, in a few words, for example "remote work" or "Christmas baking".
- **Genre:** for example article, case study, column, opinion piece, press release, report, teaser or web copy.
- **Channel:** for example website, blog, web magazine, newsletter, LinkedIn or newspaper.
- **Language:** for example `sv` or `en_GB`; this is the future text's language, independently of the language the brief is written in. If the text is to exist in several languages, give the source language and how the other versions are produced.
- **Length:** often governed by genre and channel. Give roughly how many words or characters the text should have. The length decides how much the structure can hold. If you do not know yet, give a provisional range and narrow it once the sketch is done.
- **Search phrase:** if the text is to be found through search, give the keyword or phrase it should be visible for. If the text is deliberately written without one, say so.

## 2. Which brand is the sender?

Name the brand the text is published under. In a group of companies it is rarely the group itself. Then describe the brand. If the brand has a platform, a tone-of-voice guide or another description, it is enough to link to it and write out only what governs this particular text, for example distrust that needs handling or a limit to the mandate. The tone of this text you always describe.

- **Promise:** what the brand promises its audience and wants to be known for.
- **Image:** how the reader perceives the brand today, and whether there is trust to build on or distrust to handle.
- **Mandate:** what the brand can speak about with credibility.
- **Tone of voice:** how the brand sounds.
- **Tone in this text:** the brand's tone of voice and the genre's conventions must both be respected. Where they pull in different directions, choose a compromise that sounds natural to both. If they pull the same way, say so.

## 3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?

Every text has a reason, and the reason can nearly always be put as a message. The brand's general message belongs to the description of the brand and often lies close to the promise. Here the message is that of this particular text. It may lie close to the promise, but need not. Write the message as a claim in one sentence. The message need not appear in the text. It can be conveyed indirectly, through what the text is about and where it leads the reader. But you need to know what it is, because it decides which conclusion the text should land in. An example: a company selling a tool for video meetings writes an article about remote work. The article lands in the claim that remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings. The company's message is that its tool makes the short check-ins easy. That message may never appear in the text.

## 4. Who is the reader?

Describe the typical reader of content in the chosen genre and the chosen channel. What do they already know about the topic? What do they care about? What makes them want to read this kind of content? Is there something that makes the topic particularly pressing for them right now, for example a season, a piece of news, a decision or a new figure? What you write here about why now should also show in the structure.

## 5. What is the text's angle?

The angle is the particular perspective you choose on the topic. Choose only one. The most common mistake is trying to cover the topic from every direction so that the text becomes comprehensive. The result is a text that says a little about a lot and that the reader finds hard to take in. If you see several good angles, make one text of each. You then get more texts out of the same research, and each becomes clearer. Nor does a topic ever run out. Newspapers write about Christmas baking every year. One year it is about the classics, another about biscuits without sugar and a third about baking with children. Choose the angle that lies closest to the reader and that can carry the message. The angle governs the hook, the structure and the conclusion.

## 6. What is the hook?

The hook is what makes the text interesting to the reader. It is the tension that makes the reader want to read to the end: the question, the conflict or the surprise the text promises to resolve. The hook carries the angle. In the structure, the hook becomes ABT's But or PAC's premise. The hook is not the same thing as the opening. A text can begin with a scene or a detail that catches attention, but it is the hook that holds the reader. In short texts the two often coincide. The reader still needs to understand what is at stake before the hook arrives. In a press release, the hook is the news.

## 7. How should the text be structured?

Choose a technique, or follow the genre's own form, and then sketch the text. Begin with the whole text in one sentence, in the form below for the chosen technique. Then sketch it step by step: what each step says and which facts, figures and examples carry it. The sketch is the part of the brief the writer gets most use from. Make sure the sketch fits the length the assignment gives. The technique gives the text its arc but does not decide how the content sounds. An ABT text can explain and reason, and a PAC text can contain narrative examples.

- **ABT (And, But, Therefore)** suits a text that tells: a situation and what is at stake in it, what chafes and why, and what it leads to. The And and the But come quickly to what chafes. The Therefore is the rest of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the situation] and if [...] then [...], but [the problem] because [...], therefore [...] by [...]", after Randy Olson's *Lincoln But Trump*.
- **PAC (Premise, Analysis, Conclusion)** suits a text that reasons: a question, an analysis of what the material means, and an answer. The premise comes quickly to the problem. The analysis is the largest part of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the question or starting point], and [what the analysis shows], which means that [the conclusion]", after Gordon Harvey's *Elements of the Essay* and Skolverket's *Utredande text*.
- **The genre's own form** applies to genres whose structure belongs to the genre, for example the press release. You then choose no technique but follow the form the genre states. Where a genre names an ordinary technique of its own, that technique is its form. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.
- **Free structure** suits a text where none of the forms works. Begin with an opening that catches the reader and give the main point early. Then take one step at a time, in logical order, and close with an ending that ties the text together and points forward. Sketch the steps in the order they are to be read. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.

Sketch the ending too. It ties back to the hook and shows that it is resolved, and it carries the text's call to action, directly or indirectly.

Where a genre explicitly advises against a technique, as a report does against ABT and a press release against any arc laid over its news-first order, say so with the genre's reason. A genre's ordinary technique of none is not itself advice against an arc.

## 8. What should be left out?

State boundaries, side tracks you deliberately drop, and claims you cannot substantiate. Include also what lies outside the brand's mandate or what the brand for other reasons cannot or will not say. If a boundary has exceptions, write out where the line goes, for example something that may be reported but not argued for. Refer to the brand's writing guidelines if it has any. Many boundaries become visible only once you sketch the structure.

## 9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?

The answer is the text's conclusion. Write it as a claim in one sentence, not as a topic. "Remote work" is a topic. "Remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings" is a conclusion. The conclusion is what the structure lands in, that is ABT's Therefore or PAC's Conclusion, summed up in one sentence. With the genre's own form or free structure, the conclusion is the text's main point. If it cannot be summed up in one sentence, the sketch needs sharpening. The conclusion carries the message, either by stating it or by leading the reader to it. It lies within the brand's mandate and gives the reader something worth their time. What the understanding should lead to you answer in the next question.

## 10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?

Describe the change in the reader the brand wants to bring about with the text. The conclusion is about what the reader understands. This question is about what that leads to.

- **Main effect:** choose one main effect and put it so concretely that it can be decided whether it has been reached. The effect can concern what the reader thinks or feels, for example "sees the brand as the obvious expert in the field". It can also concern what the reader does, for example "signs up for the webinar" or "contacts a salesperson".
- **The way there:** if the main effect is reached in several steps, describe what the reader first needs to see, understand or believe.
- **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team". It can also be indirect: the text does not say it, but the reader is left with the feeling that they should act and knows how. If the effect can be measured, state also what shows it has been reached, for example sign-ups, clicks or enquiries. If the text deliberately has no call to action or no measure, say so, so that it shows as a choice and not a gap.

## 11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?

This question checks that everything above serves the reader and holds together. Answer from what you have already written and state where in the structure each part is found. If something is missing there, add it now.

- **Relevant:** What makes the text relevant to the reader and their situation? Why should they read it at all? Is what makes the topic pressing right now part of the structure? The text must at least be relevant.
- **Interesting:** What makes the reader find the text interesting to read? Most often it is the hook.
- **Valuable:** What value should the text give the reader? What makes the reader feel the text was worth their time? Most often it is the conclusion and what carries it.

Then read the answers in one sweep and check that the chain holds:

- Does the reader follow from the sender and the channel?
- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle?
- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length?

content.content:
# Delivery

Every Skill that produces a Text Artifact delivers it the same way. This document is the complete contract: where a result goes, how a response carries the text, what the response carries when it went somewhere else, when a source file may be replaced instead, what happens when nothing changed, what language a run's own words about the text are written in and whether what those words say is true of the text they name, and what is refused before anything is written. It is a reference several Skills read rather than a runtime of its own. Each Skill exposes these rules through its own Formal Invocation and owns the names it gives them, so nothing here fixes how an option is spelled; what is fixed is the behaviour behind it.

## The response is the default

The default Output Target is the agent response. A run that keeps the default delivers the complete Text Artifact in the response and changes nothing on the filesystem: it creates no file, touches no file, and makes no directory. That includes scratch files and working copies of the artifact, wherever the Harness says temporary files belong.

A Harness convention identifies where an authorized temporary file belongs; it does not authorize a write. If a run genuinely needs a scratch file while composing, it removes that file before delivery and restores the filesystem to the state in which it found it. Before reporting delivery, the run checks the filesystem locations it used, including the Harness scratch area, and never reports that nothing was written while a copy of the artifact remains on disk.

An Output Target is independent of where the source material came from. Supplying a local file as source material selects no destination, and a run that reads a file still delivers to the response until the caller names somewhere else. Persisting a result is the caller's explicit choice, and making that choice is the whole of the authorization for it.

## How a response carries the text

A response carries a Text Artifact inside a fenced code block rather than as prose of the reply's own. A text and the words about it are two different things, and a reply that runs them together hands the reader a text nothing marks the edges of. Markdown is where that costs most: an artifact opening on a frontmatter delimiter, set directly beneath a paragraph the run wrote, turns that paragraph into a heading unless a blank line goes in between them — and a blank line there is what ends the frontmatter block the text was settled with. A fence removes the question rather than leaving each run to answer it, and the answers a run improvises are what made one saved reply in sixteen deliver a horizontal rule and a paragraph of configuration in place of a frontmatter block.

The complete Text Artifact sits inside exactly one fenced code block, byte for byte as the run settled it: frontmatter, blank lines and trailing structure included. Nothing is added, dropped or re-wrapped between the fence lines, and one block rather than several, a text split across two fences being a text the reader has to reassemble.

The fence is longer than the longest run of backticks inside the artifact, so a text carrying fenced code of its own cannot close it early. The info string names the text's format: `markdown` for a Markdown text, `html` for HTML, `text` for plain text.

Everything the run says *about* the text sits outside the fence — the resolved configuration, the findings and which of them are unresolved, the claim account, where a technique came from, what the run could not do. Nothing of the run's own is inside it. What the run settled as part of the document does belong inside, the Handoff Metadata and any marking the user asked to have placed in the document itself among it, because that is the text as delivered rather than a remark about it.

The rule reaches every complete text a reply carries, whether this contract calls that text delivered or not. A response-targeted run that changed nothing and has findings left fences the artifact like any other; a run that stopped before it could deliver and carries its preserved prose in the reply fences that prose, and says in its own words outside the fence what the prose has not been through. The short no-change status carries no text at all and so carries no fence. An explicit destination and In-place Editing receive the text itself and never a fence: a fence is how a reply holds a text apart from its own words, and a file has no words of its own to be held apart from.

## An explicit destination

An explicit destination is one filesystem path, and what exists at that path decides what happens to it.

**A path that does not exist** creates exactly that one file and writes the complete Text Artifact into it. Exactly one file: nothing else is created beside it, and no directory is made to hold it.

**A path naming an existing file** overwrites that exact file with the complete Text Artifact. No confirmation and no separate force option is required, and none is offered. Naming the path is the authorization, and demanding a second gesture on top of it would teach that naming a destination means something less than it says.

**A path naming an existing directory** delivers into that directory under a filename the run derives, by the rules below. Choosing a directory selects a place, not a file, so it never overwrites a file already in it.

## Deriving a filename for a directory

A directory destination needs a name, and the name comes from what the run already knows. Take the first of these the run has: the basename of the local file that supplied the Text Artifact, the title of a referenced URL, then the Skill's own working title for the text it created. Reduce it to a name the filesystem accepts, and keep a suitable text extension — the source file's own where it had one, and otherwise the one matching the text's format.

That gives a stem and an extension, and the stem stays as it is for every delivery into that directory. Where nothing exists at the derived name, that name is the file written. Where something exists there, the existing file is never overwritten: keep the original stem and take the first free numbered candidate in ascending order, beginning at `-2`. So `my-file.md`, `my-file-2.md`, `my-file-3.md` are one sequence, growing by one name at a time.

A numbered candidate is never adopted as the new stem. A third delivery into a directory already holding the first two is `my-file-3.md` and never `my-file-2-2.md`, whose stem would fork the sequence in two and leave the directory recording how many times the same text arrived rather than which arrival it was. Ascending order with the first free name also means a number freed by a deleted file is used again before a higher one is taken.

## What the response carries when a destination was named

A run that delivers to an explicit destination does not repeat the Text Artifact in the response. The response says where the text went — the derived filename included, where the destination was a directory — and carries what the file cannot: the findings the run reports beside the text, and which of them are unresolved. Naming a destination is saying where the text goes, and printing it again spends output on what the caller is already holding, doubly so when the file just written holds it too.

That holds whether or not the pass changed anything. A run that writes a file byte-identical to the source it read reports the destination and says the text needed no work, and does not become the one run that echoes a text the caller had before it started. The response is the default target precisely because a run that names no destination has nowhere else to put the artifact; naming one moves the text out of the response rather than duplicating it there.

## In-place Editing

In-place Editing replaces the single local file that supplied the Text Artifact with the result, instead of delivering it anywhere else. It is available only to a Skill whose work is to return a changed version of a text the caller already has.

A Skill that creates a new Text Artifact never edits its own source material in place. The brief, the interview, the notes, and the article it draws on are where the text came from and not where it goes; a Skill that could overwrite them would make supplying a file a risk rather than a convenience, and would lose the material the result is answerable to.

In-place Editing requires exactly one writable local source file, and it is mutually exclusive with a separate output option. A run replaces its source or delivers elsewhere, never both, and an invocation asking for both has named two destinations for one text.

It is refused wherever there is no such file to replace. Text supplied inline in the invocation or taken from the conversation is not a file. A URL is not a local file, and fetching one grants no right to write anything back. An uploaded source and a read-only file cannot be replaced. More than one Text Artifact leaves the single file the contract is written around undefined.

An explicit output path equal to the input path is refused in favour of In-place Editing, and the refusal says which gesture to use. Replacing a source then has one recognizable authorization: a reader of an invocation sees that a source is about to be replaced from the request itself, without comparing two paths to discover it.

## When nothing changed

A run may finish with nothing to change, and what it does then follows its destination.

A response-targeted run that changed nothing returns a short no-change status in place of the text when no unresolved findings remain. When findings remain, deliver the complete Text Artifact in the response and report the unresolved findings separately.

An in-place run that changed nothing leaves the source file untouched and returns the short status with any unresolved findings. Rewriting a file with its own contents would make its timestamp claim that something happened.

That status is written in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, so a Swedish text that needed no work is reported on in Swedish.

An explicitly selected different file or directory still receives the complete Text Artifact when nothing changed. Creating that artifact is what was asked for, and a destination left empty because the text needed no work is a request refused without saying so. A directory destination derives its filename and resolves collisions exactly as it would for a changed text, and the response reports the destination without repeating the artifact beside it, exactly as for a run that changed something.

## The language of a report about the text

A run that reports on the text beside the text itself — the findings it carries forward, and which of them are unresolved — writes that report in the language of the Text Artifact rather than the language of the invocation, exactly as the no-change status above is written. So a Swedish artifact reviewed from an English-language invocation comes back with Swedish findings, whether the run corrected anything or was asked to correct nothing at all, and one text never produces a status in its own language beside a finding list in another.

Who reads it is what decides this. A report about a text is read by the reader of that text, who has to finish whatever the run left undone, and a report in whichever language the invocation happened to be written in reaches that reader in a language nothing about the text promised. The invocation's language is how the run was asked for; the artifact's language is what the run is about.

## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.

## Refusals

Every contradictory, meaningless, or unusable output request is refused before the first side effect. The cases this contract names are more than one Text Artifact where the Skill processes one, an output option together with In-place Editing, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing for inline text or a URL or an uploaded or read-only source, and a destination the run cannot write — a path whose parent directory does not exist among them.

Every such check that can be made by reading is made before anything is written, so a refusal leaves no partial effect behind: no file created, none truncated, none renamed, and no directory made. Where a conflict can only be discovered after a legitimate effect, the run stops there and reports the exact partial outcome rather than continuing.

A refusal follows the Collection's ordinary diagnostic and help conventions. It names what was wrong, prints the synopsis of the most specific recognized command page verbatim, and points at that command's own help form. An output option is refused rather than ignored where it has no work to do, a flag accepted and ignored teaching that flags sometimes do nothing.

# Questions to answer before you write

The Writing Brief template: each numbered question carries the guidance for answering it. This English reference is authoritative; render its questions and guidance in the user's working language while retaining every question, its number and its order. Its genre and technique examples explain the form, not what is installed: the Library directories supply those choices, and where a genre and this guidance differ, the genre governs.

How to use the template: answer the questions in full sentences and as concretely as you can. The details under the assignment may be short. You may fill in the questions in whatever order suits you, but the order below is the one the brief is read in. It runs from what the assignment gives you, through the context and the shape of the text, to a check that everything holds together. When every answer is there, you have a brief. If you cannot answer a question, you need to find out more before you start writing. Sources and evidence, on the other hand, can be added during the work. Refer to other answers by name, for example "the message" or "the hook", not by the question's number.

## 1. What is the assignment?

Here you gather what the assignment gives you. Most of it needs no thinking up, but it governs everything that follows.

- **Working title:** a name for the text, so that everyone immediately remembers what it is about. It need not be punchy, effective or even accurate. It only needs to be short and clear.
- **Topic:** what the text is about, in a few words, for example "remote work" or "Christmas baking".
- **Genre:** for example article, case study, column, opinion piece, press release, report, teaser or web copy.
- **Channel:** for example website, blog, web magazine, newsletter, LinkedIn or newspaper.
- **Language:** for example `sv` or `en_GB`; this is the future text's language, independently of the language the brief is written in. If the text is to exist in several languages, give the source language and how the other versions are produced.
- **Length:** often governed by genre and channel. Give roughly how many words or characters the text should have. The length decides how much the structure can hold. If you do not know yet, give a provisional range and narrow it once the sketch is done.
- **Search phrase:** if the text is to be found through search, give the keyword or phrase it should be visible for. If the text is deliberately written without one, say so.

## 2. Which brand is the sender?

Name the brand the text is published under. In a group of companies it is rarely the group itself. Then describe the brand. If the brand has a platform, a tone-of-voice guide or another description, it is enough to link to it and write out only what governs this particular text, for example distrust that needs handling or a limit to the mandate. The tone of this text you always describe.

- **Promise:** what the brand promises its audience and wants to be known for.
- **Image:** how the reader perceives the brand today, and whether there is trust to build on or distrust to handle.
- **Mandate:** what the brand can speak about with credibility.
- **Tone of voice:** how the brand sounds.
- **Tone in this text:** the brand's tone of voice and the genre's conventions must both be respected. Where they pull in different directions, choose a compromise that sounds natural to both. If they pull the same way, say so.

## 3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?

Every text has a reason, and the reason can nearly always be put as a message. The brand's general message belongs to the description of the brand and often lies close to the promise. Here the message is that of this particular text. It may lie close to the promise, but need not. Write the message as a claim in one sentence. The message need not appear in the text. It can be conveyed indirectly, through what the text is about and where it leads the reader. But you need to know what it is, because it decides which conclusion the text should land in. An example: a company selling a tool for video meetings writes an article about remote work. The article lands in the claim that remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings. The company's message is that its tool makes the short check-ins easy. That message may never appear in the text.

## 4. Who is the reader?

Describe the typical reader of content in the chosen genre and the chosen channel. What do they already know about the topic? What do they care about? What makes them want to read this kind of content? Is there something that makes the topic particularly pressing for them right now, for example a season, a piece of news, a decision or a new figure? What you write here about why now should also show in the structure.

## 5. What is the text's angle?

The angle is the particular perspective you choose on the topic. Choose only one. The most common mistake is trying to cover the topic from every direction so that the text becomes comprehensive. The result is a text that says a little about a lot and that the reader finds hard to take in. If you see several good angles, make one text of each. You then get more texts out of the same research, and each becomes clearer. Nor does a topic ever run out. Newspapers write about Christmas baking every year. One year it is about the classics, another about biscuits without sugar and a third about baking with children. Choose the angle that lies closest to the reader and that can carry the message. The angle governs the hook, the structure and the conclusion.

## 6. What is the hook?

- **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team".
